72c354752ae0299a: Coca-Cola is using AI to recommend which products Malaysian retailers should order and in what quantities through its Coke Buddy platform.
The Perfect Basket feature uses Coca-Cola’s Central Recommendation Engine to analyse previous orders, ordering frequency, seasonality, weather, and purchasing patterns among similar businesses.

Coca-Cola said Coke Buddy currently supports about 39,000 retail outlets across Malaysia. The company describes Coke Buddy as a self-ordering platform that allows retailers to buy products through its app, website, or WhatsApp, with personalised order suggestions and order tracking also available.

Perfect Basket builds on those existing ordering functions by recommending both products and quantities before a retailer completes an order. Retailers can review the recommendations and retain control over what they purchase.
How Perfect Basket guides retailer orders

Coke Buddy already uses previous purchase history to suggest products a retailer is likely to order again. Perfect Basket adds other signals, including seasonality, weather, ordering frequency, and purchasing trends among comparable businesses.

Perfect Basket recommends products and quantities before retailers submit their orders through Coke Buddy. Fulfilment is handled separately by Coca-Cola Refreshments Malaysia or its suppliers under existing sales and distribution arrangements.
Coca-Cola said its sales teams remain involved with retailers alongside the digital ordering system, while retailers retain control over the final purchasing decision.

Coca-Cola recently disclosed usage figures for Perfect Basket following its Perfect Basket, Perfect Ride campaign, which ran from January to April 2026. The campaign encouraged retailers to use the recommendation feature when placing orders and received more than 4,500 entries from over 4,000 retailers in Malaysia.

During the campaign, 83% of participating outlets adopted Perfect Basket recommendations, according to Coca-Cola. The figure applies only to retailers taking part in the campaign, not the full network of about 39,000 outlets supported by Coke Buddy.

Coca-Cola also said participating outlets that followed the recommendations recorded higher sales revenue growth than comparable retail outlets. The company did not disclose the size of the difference or provide detailed performance data showing how individual recommendations affected sales or inventory levels.
The available Malaysian campaign data does not provide figures for forecast accuracy, stock availability, inventory levels, or logistics costs.
Suggested orders extend beyond Malaysia

Coca-Cola has deployed similar suggested-order capabilities elsewhere in its bottling network. In its first-quarter 2024 results, the company said it and its bottling partners had connected nearly eight million customers to B2B platforms globally, while AI-enabled suggested-order capabilities had reached more than three million outlets in Latin America.

Coca-Cola has said these systems combine customer data, external information, and AI to generate predictive order recommendations. Then-chief executive James Quincey said in 2024 that digital ordering also allows retailers to adjust deliveries without waiting for a salesperson to visit.

Coca-Cola has also linked suggested orders to changes in its sales process. Quincey said AI-generated orders allow pre-sales staff to spend less time taking routine orders and more time on account development, while retailers continue to make the final purchasing decision.

Coca-Cola has reported results from earlier pilots using similar recommendation systems. In its second-quarter 2024 earnings call, the company said retailers receiving AI-generated product recommendations based on previous orders and market data were more than 30% more likely to purchase the recommended SKUs in initial pilots. These results did not relate specifically to Perfect Basket in Malaysia.

In a separate demand-prediction project, Coca-Cola combined historical sales data with weather and geolocation information to generate replenishment recommendations. CIO Neeraj Tolmare told Fortune in 2025 that a three-country pilot recorded sales 7% to 8% higher than outlets that were not using the AI algorithm.

Perfect Basket remains available after the campaign. Coca-Cola said it plans to continue developing Coke Buddy and the recommendation feature using retailer feedback and data, while retailers will continue to have access to the company’s sales representatives alongside the digital ordering system.

10312401d4c3c755: Google’s newest AI weather forecasting model predicts wind speed at 100 metres above the ground, roughly the height of a modern wind turbine. It also forecasts cloud cover and how much sunlight reaches the surface, and it updates every hour. Energy traders, grid operators and wind and solar developers already pay other companies for that data. The introduction of WeatherNext 3 now puts Google in their market.

Google DeepMind and Google Research released the model on September 3. It produces a global forecast every hour at up to five-kilometre resolution for surface variables such as temperature and moisture. The previous version, WeatherNext 2, worked on a 25-kilometre grid and refreshed every six hours. Google says the new energy variables are meant to help grid operators and developers predict how much power their wind and solar assets will generate, then match that against demand.

The consumer side of the launch has had most of the attention. WeatherNext 3 now powers weather results in Google Search, the Gemini app, Google Maps and the Google Maps Platform Weather API. Behind it sits an enterprise layer that matters more commercially. The same forecast data can be queried in BigQuery and Earth Engine or downloaded in bulk from Google Cloud Storage, with no model setup required by the customer.
Why the energy sector is buying AI weather forecasting

Grid operators are running a system that has become harder to predict at both ends. On the generation side, renewables now account for most new capacity. S&P Global Market Intelligence’s US Grid Outlook 2026 projects solar and energy storage as the primary sources of new capacity this year, at 51.2GW and 25.7GW respectively out of more than 90GW of planned additions.
Solar and wind generate according to the weather rather than demand, so each gigawatt added makes a short-term forecast more accurate.

On the consumption side, the new load is coming from AI. S&P Global identifies the spread of data centres across North America as a primary driver of the recent surge in electricity demand, forcing utilities to revise their load forecasts upward. Deloitte’s 2026 Power and Utilities Industry Outlook projects peak demand growing by roughly 26% by 2035, with data centre demand alone potentially reaching 176GW, five times its 2024 level.

The cost of getting a forecast wrong is straightforward. If an operator underestimates how much wind power will arrive, it has to buy replacement electricity at short notice, usually from gas plants kept on expensive standby. If it overestimates, wind and solar farms end up being paid to switch off because the grid cannot absorb what they are producing. Both outcomes are expensive, and both are forecasting failures.
The market Google is entering

Selling weather forecasts to the energy sector is an established business. Vaisala, Solcast, DNV’s WindGEMINI and IBM’s HyperWatch all compete in it. So does Jua, a Swiss firm that claims its EPT-2 model beats Microsoft Aurora and DeepMind’s earlier GraphCast on accuracy while updating 24 times a day, against what it describes as a typical four updates a day among competitors.

Google’s advantage is reach. The same forecast appears as a table in BigQuery, a layer in Earth Engine, an API in Google Maps Platform and the default answer in Google Search. No specialist vendor has that spread, and the hourly refresh closes the update-frequency gap those vendors have used to differentiate themselves.

The incumbents have one technical argument left. Jua’s published position is that physics-based models such as ECMWF’s HRES still outperform purely data-driven AI models during record-breaking extreme weather, because physics models encode rules about how energy and mass move through the atmosphere, while AI models learn patterns from past data.

Jua sells a physics-constrained product, so the claim serves its own interests. It also describes the conditions grid operators worry about most, when a storm falls outside anything the model has seen in training.
What is new, and what is being oversold

The architectural claim behind WeatherNext 3 is that it learns from real observations instead of from simulations. Most AI weather models, WeatherNext 2 included, are trained on output from numerical weather prediction models, which are supercomputer-driven physics simulations that carry a six-hour data lag. That lag can introduce bias in fast-changing variables such as rain and surface temperature. WeatherNext 3 ingests live geostationary satellite imagery and trains directly on readings from individual weather stations.

The shift is real, though narrower than much of the coverage has suggested. Google’s own system diagram shows the model taking in one-hour satellite mosaics alongside traditional historical analysis. DeepMind senior research scientist Ilan Price told Bloomberg the gain comes from not waiting for the next analysis and using the most recent information available instead.
Reporting puts the remaining data lag at three to four hours, down from about seven. Dependence on numerical weather prediction has been reduced, not removed.

The accuracy figures need similar care. Google reports improvements of up to 60% against NASA’s IMERG satellite product, 30% against MRMS radar and 10% against rain gauge readings at early lead times, measured using a standard scoring method for probability forecasts. Those are three separate baselines, and the percentages do not add together. The widely repeated claim of 50% better precipitation forecasting applies specifically to forecasts a day or more ahead. Every figure carries an “up to” qualifier, which makes each one a best case rather than a typical result.

Google published no independent third-party validation alongside the launch. It points instead to live evaluations by Brightband, whose leaderboard it cites in claiming WeatherNext 3 is the most accurate global weather model to date. A utility considering a switch away from a paid specialist will care more about performance in its own service territory, on its own assets, than about a global leaderboard position.
Google’s own stake in the problem

Google is selling forecasting tools into a grid problem its own industry helped create. The data centre build-out driving the load growth utilities are struggling to serve is led by the hyperscalers, Google among them, and Google has signed multi-gigawatt renewable procurement agreements to supply its own facilities.

Accurate prediction of wind and solar output is directly useful to a company matching large volumes of clean energy against a load that is both growing and variable. That is commercial logic, and it goes some way to explaining why the energy variables shipped in this release.

Google has not published pricing for enterprise access to WeatherNext 3, or said whether the BigQuery and Earth Engine data carries standard Cloud query charges or a separate licence. Utilities weighing a move away from a paid specialist will want that figure before they weigh any accuracy claim.
2025, more than 65,000 employees in its Corporate and Investment Bank were actively using the platform, while more than 90% of its engineers were using AI coding assistants.
The bank also said AI-based transaction screening allowed it to review more than twice the previous transaction volume while reducing manual operator checks by half.

Bank of America is using a generative AI-enabled system called EricaAssist with more than 18,000 customer service employees. The tool summarises why a customer is calling, retrieves relevant information, and recommends possible next steps while keeping the employee responsible for the interaction.

Bank of America said in July 2026 that EricaAssist can deliver contextual guidance in under three seconds and has reduced average call times by nearly one minute. The bank plans to extend the system to additional servicing scenarios and business lines later in 2026.

b7399b7d2cf80384: YouTube was the most frequently cited website in Google AI Overviews across a panel of vitamin and supplement searches, according to new research. The video platform appeared in 186 of 350 AI-generated answers, or 53.1%, making it the only website cited in more than half of the answers collected.

Searcherries followed 50 searches daily from August 30 to September 5, 2026. The questions came from Google Autocomplete and covered topics including hair growth, energy, sleep, anxiety and weight loss. Every search produced an AI Overview, the AI-generated summary that Google displays alongside its search results.

GoodRx was the second most frequently cited website, appearing in 48.3% of answers. Healthline followed at 28.6%, Cleveland Clinic at 28.0%, and the National Institutes of Health domain, nih.gov, at 25.1%. Websites were ranked by the number of answers citing them, with each website counted only once per answer.

YouTube’s presence extended across 44 of the 50 queries. It was particularly prominent in the group beginning with “vitamins for,” appearing in 78.6% of those answers. Across the full panel, YouTube appeared almost twice as often as Healthline.

The research also found that AI Overviews frequently cited pages outside the recorded organic results. Only 32.4% of cited pages appeared in the organic listings collected for the same search; 67.6% did not. Matching by website instead of exact page raised the overlap to 52.5%, showing that some AI citations pointed to a different page on a website already present in organic search.

Individual answers were less consistent than the overall leaderboard. For “supplements for weight loss,” nih.gov appeared every day and YouTube appeared on six of seven days, while other websites moved in and out. By contrast, “supplements to help with glp-1 side effects” returned the same cited pages throughout the week.

Searcherries monitored a fixed set of 50 Google Autocomplete queries once daily using US English desktop results configured for New York. The analysis covered 350 AI Overviews and 5,036 citation occurrences across 572 distinct pages and 218 websites. Organic overlap was calculated within each search, counting repeated citations to the same page once; the recorded organic lists contained seven to ten results.
9df2a000d362ff4f: Baru-baru ini saya menonton kembali filem Kala Malam Bulan Mengambang arahan Mamat Khalid. Kali pertama saya menontonnya ialah ketika filem itu ditayangkan di pawagam. Saya tak ingat tahun berapa sehinggalah selepas disemak kembali, rupanya pada 2008. Maknanya sudah hampir dua dekad.

Entah kenapa filem ini sedikit tenggelam apabila orang bercakap tentang karya Mamat Khalid. Kita lebih mudah mengingati Rock, Zombi Kampung Pisang, Hantu Kak Limah dan segala macam watak serta dialog daripada filem-filemnya yang sudah masuk dalam budaya popular sedangkan Kala Malam Bulan Mengambang pun sedap juga.

Setelah menontonnya kembali hampir 20 tahun kemudian, saya rasa filem ini memberitahu sesuatu tentang Mamat Khalid yang kelihatannya terlindung di sebalik reputasi beliau sebagai pengarah komedi -- mamat ini sangat faham bahasa sinema.

Ironinya, Kala Malam Bulan Mengambang bukanlah filem yang tidak dihargai ketika zamannya. Pada Festival Filem Malaysia ke-21 (2008), filem ini memenangi Filem Terbaik, Pengarah Terbaik untuk Mamat Khalid dan Pelakon Lelaki Terbaik menerusi Rosyam Nor, selain Penataan Seni Terbaik dan Pereka Kostum/Busana Terbaik. Pada Anugerah Skrin tahun yang sama, ia turut memenangi Filem Terbaik, Pengarah Terbaik dan Pelakon Lelaki Terbaik.

Jadi ini bukan perihal filem yang gagal kemudian kita sengaja mahu angkat semula. Tak! Ia pernah diraikan. Cuma entah bagaimana, apabila masa berlalu dan nama Mamat Khalid semakin besar, filem ini seperti tersorok sedikit di belakang karya-karya beliau yang lain. Mungkin kerana Kala Malam Bulan Mengambang agak aneh. Atau penonton kita jarang didedahkan dengan konsep komedi yang pelbagai dalam filem Melayu, malah kita pun tak begitu mahir yang komedi ada banyak cabang.

Yang kita selalu nampak, 'kelakar' hanyalah gelak ketawa dengan dialog, aksi serta mimik wajah yang bersekali. Kita tak tahu komedi ada 'slapstick', situation comedy (sitcom), 'deadpan', dark comedy dan satu dua lagi. Apatah lagi konsep 'noir' dalam filem Melayu yang memang asing.

Kala Malam Bulan Mengambang -- filem yang dibuat dalam hitam putih ini membawa kita ke sebuah pekan pada zaman 1950-an bersama Saleh (lakonan Rosyam Nor), seorang wartawan yang terjebak dalam satu misteri. Ada pembunuhan, watak-watak misteri, jembalang dan harimau jadian, orang-orang pelik dan suasana yang kadang-kadang membuatkan kita tidak pasti sama ada Mamat sedang serius atau sedang mengenakan kita. Rupanya kedua-duanya.

Malah ada beberapa babak membuat saya ketawa lebih panjang berbanding saya menonton filem-filem komedi lain karya beliau terutama bila mendengarkan 'voice over' Saleh; ketika dia mengejar seseorang, kerap dia merungut tentang kesukaran dia berlari laju kerana penyakit angin pasang yang dihidapinya.

Pada permukaannya kita boleh mengatakan Mamat sedang bermain dengan filem noir, genre yang kita kenal melalui filem detektif lama Hollywood -- permainan cahaya dan bayang. Tetapi Mamat tidak sekadar meminjam teknik Hollywood. Dia mencampurkannya dengan suasana filem Melayu studio zaman dahulu dengan mengadunkan unsur seram, melodrama dan perangai orang kita sendiri.

Sebab itu saya kata Mamat faham bahasa sinema dan budaya sendiri. Ada beberapa babak dia 'membantai' perangai orang kita. Karyawan yang mahu bermain dan melanggar sesuatu genre terlebih dahulu perlulah memahami genre yang hendak dipersendakannya. Maka itu, adunan kesemua resipi itu mencipta satu identiti iaitu 'filem Mamat Khalid'. Hitam putihnya bukan sekadar supaya nampak klasik. Kostum, bangunan, kedai, kenderaan, cahaya, muzik, cara manusia berdiri malah cara mereka bercakap semuanya membantu membina sebuah dunia. Kita boleh mengambil satu babak tanpa mengetahui tajuk filemnya dan rasanya tetap ada cap dagang Mamat pada gambar itu. Ini sisi Mamat yang kadang-kadang tenggelam kerana kita terlalu mengingatinya melalui lawak.

Dalam Kala Malam Bulan Mengambang, perkara itu jelas. Ia filem misteri, komedi, seram, parodi dan satira dalam satu masa. Saya pernah baca, ada pengkaji dan pengkritik filem mentafsir lebih jauh sindiran politik dan sosial di dalamnya, termasuk simbol-simbol tertentu seperti bulan dan keris yang dikaitkan dengan kuasa, masyarakat serta industri filem sendiri. Mamat juga melalui dialog Saleh, selamba menyentuh tentang perjuangan komunis yang sia-sia dan tidak mendapat tempat di Malaysia.

Saya tidak mahu pergi sejauh itu. Kalau semua benda hendak dicari simbolnya, nanti tengok keris kita takut, tengok bulan kita gelabah, macam kita fobia dengan simbol mata dan segi tiga. Tetapi memang terasa Mamat menggunakan dunia lama untuk bercakap tentang dunia semasanya. Semuanya dimasukkan ke dalam dunia pelik yang dibinanya. Bagi mereka yang selalu menyangka filem adalah dunia realiti, pasti akan menemui kepayahan jika menonton filem ini.

Saya juga pernah terbaca yang Kala Malam Bulan Mengambang agak berserabut dan terlalu banyak perkara mahu dimasukkan. Ada pengkritik juga melihat, apabila cerita semakin berkembang, ia mula melemah dan kurang meyakinkan seperti bagaimana permulaan ceritanya. Akibatnya, keghairahan untuk menonton sampai habis pun mengendur. Tetapi setelah menontonnya kembali baru-baru ini, saya boleh pula meleraikan keserabutan itu. Ini kerana ada pengkritik filem juga pernah berkata, kita tak semestinya perlu memahami cerita sesebuah filem itu sekiranya kita seronok menontonnya. Cukup kita menikmatinya sahaja. Saya setuju. Kala Malam Bulan Mengambang adalah filem yang cukup sekadar kita nikmatinya, tak payah susah-susah memahaminya. Cuma, apa yang boleh saya kata ialah Mamat Khalid adalah genius sinema.

Selepas pemergiannya pada 2021, kita semakin sedar betapa banyak watak dan dialog ciptaannya sudah menjadi sebahagian budaya popular. Orang masih menyebut Kampung Pisang. Orang masih mengulang dialog Hantu Kak Limah. Watak daripada dunia Rock masih dikenali. Man Laksa dirindukan. Itu pencapaian besar seorang pembikin filem. Mamat Khalid berjaya mengubah suatu kebiasaan. Orang masuk panggung mahu tonton cerita yang dibuat Mamat Khalid, bukan sangat hendak melihat muka-muka yang kacak lawa. Mamat Khalid berjaya mempopularkan pelakon-pelakon 'muka awam' (istilah orang sekarang) dalam filem-filem yang selalu menjadi sebutan ramai itu.

Cuma sesekali elok juga kita berjalan keluar sedikit dari Kampung Pisang untuk melihat karya Mamat yang ini. Di dalam Kala Malam Bulan Mengambang, kita mungkin akan bertemu Mamat Khalid yang sedikit berbeza daripada yang selalu kita kenang. Ini Mamat yang menunjukkan bahawa di sebalik segala lawaknya, dia seorang pencinta filem yang tahu bagaimana gambar, cahaya, bunyi, ruang, watak dan genre boleh digunakan untuk bercerita. Mamat telah membuktikan betapa luasnya dunia sinema untuk dipelbagaikan dalam sesebuah karya.

Filem Kala Malam Bulan Mengambang seperti sengaja dibuat hitam putih oleh Mamat supaya kelihatan seperti sebuah filem lama. Dan kini setelah hampir dua dekad, ia benar-benar menjadi sebuah filem lama. Pernah diiktiraf dengan anugerah tetapi ternyata ia telah dilupakan. Itu ironinya. Entah-entah memang ironi ini telah dijangka oleh Mamat. Agaknyalah! Kalau benar -- saya suka ironi ini.

a7697c4dfda2d66c: From Terence Netto
For nearly two decades now Abdul Rahman Kassim of PAS has been striving to better ties between his party and Christian groups in the north of the Peninsula.
His efforts have taken the form of organising dialogue sessions between his party’s leaders and priests and lay activists of mainly the Catholic Church in northern Perak, Kedah and Penang.

When Sebastian Francis became Bishop of Penang in 2013, Rahman found in the bishop, who was elevated to the office of cardinal in 2023, a ready interlocutor between Islamists like him and the Catholic Church.

Get-to-know-you sessions, dialogues, high teas, lunches, dinners and visits to architecturally interesting mosques, were organised by Rahman and his cohort for the edification of their Catholic counterparts.
Sebastian and his entourage, which included on occasion this scribe, were, at times, transfixed by the hospitality and goodwill exuded by their hosts.
With the vibes that good, Christian-Muslim relations appeared to be a cinch, but this reporter was sceptical because their theologies clashed on several fronts, too stark to ignore.
But Rahman, an optimist who declines to dwell on the problematic, is unfazed by these contradictions.
Once he even invited Cardinal Sebastian to grace his daughter’s wedding held at his home in Tasek Gelugor, Penang.

The prelate accepted the invitation, mingling and talking with Rahman’s guests during dinner, causing no small amount of surprise and delight among people unused to seeing a crucifix-wearing personage of the church at ease in their midst.

A PAS activist of more than four decades’ involvement, 70-year-old Rahman has shown no interest in scaling the party hierarchy which is probably why his colleagues view his exertions in promoting Muslim-Christian ties as something to be welcomed.
Rahman also knows that Sebastian is due for retirement at the end of this year when he reaches the church’s mandatory retirement age of 75.
Rahman had set, as a goal of his two decade-long effort at outreach to Christians, the cardinal’s acceptance of an invitation to attend the 72nd muktamar in Kota Bharu.

He wasn’t sure Sebastian would accept the invitation knowing that though the prelate’s jurisdiction as Bishop of Penang included Kelantan, he is too busy with church matters to find time for non-ecclesiastical affairs.

f1e3b4a2a08906cf: "I cannot."
With those two words, a golf club security manager laid bare a problem that haunts every courtroom, every tender and every audit in Malaysia.

S Saravanan, group security head of Tropicana Golf & Country Resort, was testifying on Sept 1 in the corruption trial of former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin. The club's computer records showed Muhyiddin had played golf with businessman Azman Yusoff on July 19, 2020, a date that matters to the case.

Then came the cross-examination. Could he vouch for the accuracy of the information in the system? "I cannot," he admitted. When defence counsel pressed that "it can be modified", the best Saravanan could offer was "I am not sure about that".
And just like that, the record wobbled. Not because anyone proved tampering, but because nobody could prove there was none.

This is not one trial's problem. On Aug 27, Malaysians witnessed a spectacle no country would envy: three former prime ministers, Najib Razak, Muhyiddin Yassin and Ismail Sabri Yaakob, at the Kuala Lumpur Court Complex on the same day for separate proceedings.

Najib faced a US$5.64 billion (RM22.8 billion) civil suit brought by 1MDB; Muhyiddin's trial over charges of soliciting RM225.3 million in bribes for Bersatu continued, charges he is contesting; and Ismail Sabri pleaded not guilty to failing to declare assets to the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC). The courts will decide each case on their merits.

But every one of these cases turns on records. Bank statements, procurement papers, approval chains, logbooks. And the first move of any defence is to ask the same devastating question: how do you know this record was not changed?

It is a fair question. Almost every record the Malaysian state relies on, from tender evaluations in ePerolehan, the finance ministry's e-procurement system, to departmental expenditure files, lives in an ordinary database.
An ordinary database can be edited by whoever holds the administrator password. History, in other words, belongs to whoever controls the server.

Here is where blockchain technology can earn its keep. Not the meme-coin casino that has soured many on the word, but something far more boring and far more useful: a public logbook that nobody, not even the government, can rewrite.

The mechanics are simple. Every time a record is created - a bid submitted, a score entered, an award signed - the system generates its cryptographic hash, a unique digital fingerprint, and publishes that fingerprint to a blockchain. The record itself stays private; only the fingerprint goes public.
If anyone later alters so much as a comma, the fingerprint no longer matches. Tampering does not become impossible. It becomes instantly detectable, by anyone, forever.

Let me be honest about what this cannot do. A blockchain cannot verify that a record was true when it was written; log the wrong 15 names and the wrong 15 names are preserved for eternity. Nor will it stop cash in envelopes or phone calls that never touch a system.

But look at what it kills: backdating, quiet edits, vanishing files, doctored evaluations. The cover-up, in short. In court, it transforms the question from "can this record be trusted?", which no witness can answer, into "has this record changed since the day it was made?", which mathematics answers.

This is not theory. Estonia became the first country to run blockchain in live government systems in 2012, and today its land registry, business registry, state gazette and more than a million health records are anchored this way.

The World Economic Forum and the Inter-American Development Bank have trialled a blockchain procurement system for Colombia's school meals programme, complete with automatic red flags for suspicious bids.

Malaysia does not even need to build the rails. The Malaysia Blockchain Infrastructure, developed by national research agency MIMOS Berhad with MY EG Services and powered by the Zetrix chain, has been operational since April 2025. What is missing is the mandate. Three moves would supply it.

First, anchor procurement. The finance ministry should require ePerolehan to hash every tender milestone, submission, evaluation score and award decision to the national blockchain the moment each occurs.

Azam Baki, in his final days as MACC chief commissioner this May, put procurement and public fund leakages at an estimated RM277 billion over six years, warning: "We cannot afford to slow down. Corruption in this country is still serious and in certain sectors it is systemic."

Second, wire in the Auditor-General. Give the National Audit Department live, read-only access to anchored expenditure logs, turning audits from post-mortems into continuous monitoring. The Auditor-General's first report for 2026 flagged 273 new financial and governance issues. Catching them as they happen beats cataloguing them years later.

Third, update the Evidence Act 1950. Section 90A admits computer records on a certificate that were produced in the course of ordinary use, a presumption any sharp lawyer can shake, as Tuesday showed. A cryptographic proof of integrity should stand alongside it, so court time is spent arguing the case, not the logbook.

Malaysia's score on Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index rose to 52 this year, lifting us to 54th place and third in Asean. Enforcement is working. But records that cannot be quietly rewritten would harden the entire system by protecting the innocent and cornering the guilty.
No witness should again be left saying "I cannot" while justice hangs on a database. The technology is proven and the losses are counted. What Putrajaya needs now is the will.

d5ca18d43799b83b: US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh is convinced, and prominent economists agree, that AI will meaningfully increase labour productivity. Don’t bet on it. In fact, wider adoption of these models could reduce output per worker.
Widespread adoption of new technologies is a cornerstone of economic dynamism. And in the internet era, accessible user interfaces and affordability have been indispensable enablers.
Until the early 1990s, technical wizards relied on rigidly structured, text-based tools like Gopher to exchange documents on the internet.
Then, the more flexible World Wide Web emerged, spawning browsers—Mosaic, Netscape Navigator, and Microsoft’s Internet Explorer—and search engines that were quick, easy-to-use, and cheap.

AltaVista, the first “full-text” searchable index of the World Wide Web, went from receiving 300,000 hits on its first day in 1995 to more than 80 million daily hits. But AltaVista defaced its results with ugly banners.
So, when Google launched its search engine in 1998, users like me fell for its design, without regard to the quality of its results.

Google’s success crushed rival search engines and traditional print publishers, and its engineers miraculously maintained the efficiency of computing infrastructure to ensure that searching for information remained quick, easy, and cheap.
But success also then undermined user experience and productivity. As Google became a monopolist, search-engine optimisers flooded results with useless links. Traditional media resorted to clickbait.

This flotsam forced users to learn new skills: how to select keywords, use Boolean operators (like “AND”), and recognise clickbait. Google further degraded the experience by displaying “sponsored” results at the top of the page.

AI chatbots have followed a similar path. ChatGPT attracted a million users in its first five days after its launch in November 2022. As with Google’s initially clean search page, the chatbot’s interface was compelling: users could ask questions in plain English, no Boolean operators required.

Unfortunately, ChatGPT turned out to be a mendacious talking horse. Filtering out its fabrications took more time than conducting keyword searches on Google, reducing productivity. Bard—the chatbot that Google, facing an existential threat to its search dominance, rushed to release—was equally disappointing.

Now, more than three years later, Google has shut down Bard and replaced it with both an “AI overview” above its traditional search results and an AI Mode option—a chatbot that urges users to “ask anything”. In my experience, though, the results remain maddeningly unreliable, even for simple queries.

Compared to traditional statistical models, including Google’s pioneering algorithms, large language models (LLMs) appear to offer compelling advantages. With trillions of parameters, LLMs can incorporate contextual factors that earlier models had to ignore.
And LLMs do not merely inform; they use metaphors and humour in what the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein called “language-games” that reassure, explain, flatter, assert, and cajole.

Like their earlier counterparts, however, LLMs rely on statistical extrapolation, assuming futures that repeat the past. That is fine for natural phenomena like protein folding, but not for ever-changing goods and services.

Small modifications to the layout of a laptop battery, for example, can make instructions on how to replace it useless. Despite this, users—like the participants in Stanley Milgram’s notorious shock experiments—reflexively obey a chatbot’s confident answer.

By contrast, traditional search links are better at displaying the outdatedness of information and the unreliability of sources. This gives users more discretion to exercise their judgment, which reduces misfires and costs.

Indiscriminately including trillions of parameters magnifies LLMs’ extrapolation problems by increasing the likelihood that they will find nonexistent patterns or select irrelevant or unreliable answers from exhaustive, uncurated catalogues. Designers of traditional statistical models can restrict variables and data sources to avoid that outcome while controlling computational costs.

LLMs’ reliance on statistical extrapolation also makes their conversational interfaces linguistic chimeras. Because LLMs cannot replicate human sense-making and have no real contextual understanding of intent, they do not use language as a “form of life,” to borrow from Wittgenstein again.

The pretense that they do has enabled AI peddlers to push chatbots indiscriminately, especially as the narrower applications for which LLMs are actually useful cannot justify multi-trillion-dollar investments.

AI pushers are going all out to addict people. Google’s AI overviews and AI Mode are like a free taste. Once users are hooked, hyperscalers will surely charge high prices to recoup their steep development and operating costs.
One might hope that even the most powerful firms cannot dupe consumers into submission. Despite seemingly unlimited resources, Google has had at least as many flops as hits.

Meta’s very name memorialises a failed multi-billion-dollar bet on virtual reality. But the marketing blitz that has turned junk-food addiction into a booming business provides a disheartening counter-example.

Hyperscalers could make LLM addiction as widespread as physiological addictions by exploiting humans’ deep-seated desire for companionable conversation. As social ties fray, chatbots offer a simulacrum, potentially turning serious professionals into lovesick teenagers.

And as with other addictions, LLMs are already usurping resources—including capital, electricity, chips, and entrepreneurial energy—that other deserving innovations need. As this continues, techno-optimists should rethink their rosy view of AI’s productivity promise.
Amar Bhidé is professor of health policy at Columbia University’s Mailman School of Public Health.

f25d3fe06b1d41da: MG Ship has introduced an AI route optimisation and carrier selection module as logistics deployments demonstrate rapid cost and time returns.

The technical module targets global retailers and commercial shippers, pairing automated routing algorithms with carrier recommendation systems across international trade corridors. The deployment arrives as enterprise supply chain operators report measurable operational returns from machine learning tools, moving capital allocations away from speculative trials toward production deployments.
Measurable returns from deploying AI for logistics

Suki Cheung, CEO of MG Ship, will present deployment metrics during a panel discussion at the upcoming WMX Asia conference. Cheung will join executives from Pos Malaysia, Omniva, and OnyX Space for the session, titled AI Beyond the Hype: Measurable Results in Logistics Today.

“Too many AI conversations in logistics remain focused on future possibilities,” said Cheung. “The reality is that AI is already delivering measurable business outcomes today. Leading organisations are reducing transportation costs, improving forecast accuracy, increasing warehouse productivity, and achieving payback within months rather than years.”
Industry operational data indicates that initial investment returns are concentrating across three primary workflows:

Dynamic route planning has reduced enterprise fuel consumption by 15–20 percent, improved transit speeds by 15–25 percent, and lowered overall transportation costs by 12–22 percent, with capital payback reached within three to six months.
Predictive demand forecasting has reduced projection errors by 20–40 percent, improved planning accuracy by up to 35 percent, and decreased excess inventory by 20–30 percent within six to 12 months.
Automated freight documentation processing has cut manual task duration by up to 85 percent, recovering initial expenditure inside three to six months.
Over five-year deployment cycles, enterprise adopters have recorded average operational expense reductions between 10–25 percent, accompanied by warehouse productivity gains of 25–35 percent.
Routing algorithms and carrier scoring

MG Ship built the new routing capability directly into its visibility and supply chain intelligence platform, which serves retailers, manufacturers, and freight operators across multiple international markets. The base system synthesises live cargo telemetry with trade intelligence, risk monitoring, and predictive analytics to support operational planning and trade financing.

The route optimisation engine processes live and historical lane transit logs, weather patterns, air and ocean port congestion indicators, customs risk alerts, and transit reliability data. Shippers receive automated recommendations identifying low-cost, low-risk transit paths.

Carrier evaluation features rank transport providers per lane and service tier. Rather than selecting capacity purely on spot freight pricing, the system scores carriers against historical on-time metrics, transit consistency, exception occurrences, claims rates, available volume, and total cost-to-serve.

Logistics teams can also execute scenario simulations prior to peak shipping quarters. The software models lead times, service levels, freight spend, and risk exposures under alternative carrier allocation rules.
Early enterprise implementations demonstrate lower lead-time variance, reduced expedited freight expenditure, and improved on-time-in-full delivery rates.

Cheung stated that the platform “does not simply tell businesses where their cargo is”, adding that “it recommends the best route, the right carrier, and the lowest-risk option based on real-time conditions, helping organisations make faster and more profitable decisions.”

efdb90da74008909: From Nurul Anna Mausar
As Sabah woke up today, the haze was still here.
At 7am, Kota Kinabalu recorded an air pollutant index of 153, placing it in the “unhealthy” category.
The reading follows another difficult weekend for Sabah, with Kota Kinabalu and Kimanis recording unhealthy API readings of 157 and 151, respectively, on Sunday.
Sabah's environment department has attributed the haze to transboundary smoke from forest and peatland fires in Kalimantan.
For many Sabahans, however, haze is not simply a number on an air-quality application.

It is the grey sky we wake up to. The outdoor plans we cancel. The children we worry about sending outside. The workers who cannot simply choose to stay indoors. It is the uncomfortable feeling of knowing that the air we breathe is polluted, even when we have done nothing to cause it.
For Sabah, haze is not a distant environmental crisis. We breathe it, too.
Yet, whenever transboundary haze returns, the conversation often devolves into pointing fingers across borders.
It is easy to blame Indonesia. But that is neither sufficient nor particularly helpful.

Communities in Kalimantan are breathing the same smoke. They, too, are losing access to clean air and suffering the consequences of the fires. Borneo's forests, peatlands and weather systems do not recognise the political borders between Malaysia and Indonesia.
But recognising this shared vulnerability does not mean abandoning accountability.
In fact, it should make us ask a much more uncomfortable question: who is actually benefitting from the burning?
If forests and peatlands are deliberately burned to clear land for commercial purposes, Asean governments cannot afford to stop their investigations at the person who physically starts the fire.
They need to follow the land. Follow the concession. Follow the ownership. Follow the money.
Ultimately, they need to ask: where are the companies, directors and CEOs who profit from these operations?

Indonesia has already identified 19 companies whose concession areas were affected by fires covering more than 11,000 hectares. Authorities are investigating whether the fires were accidental or deliberate, while maintaining that strict liability applies when a fire occurs within a concession area.
Yet the companies have not been publicly named.
This is where Asean's response needs to become more ambitious.

If deliberate burning is taking place on corporate-controlled land, accountability should not end with a farmer, worker or contractor on the ground. The person holding the match may start the fire, but the people who profit from the land deserve scrutiny, too.
That does not mean automatically declaring every company guilty. It means demanding transparency, proper investigations and consequences where evidence establishes responsibility.

Civil society groups in Malaysia have already called for Indonesia to disclose concession maps, fire investigation findings and ownership information so that potentially implicated companies, including Malaysian-linked companies, can be investigated in Malaysia as well.
This is precisely the kind of cross-border cooperation Asean should be strengthening.

The Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution has existed for more than two decades. Yet every haze season, we seem to return to the same cycle: monitor the hotspots, issue health advisories, conduct firefighting operations, wait for the rain, and hope the problem goes away.
That is not a long-term solution.

Asean needs stronger mechanisms for sharing satellite data, identifying the ownership of affected concessions, investigating corporate actors and enforcing environmental responsibilities across borders.

Malaysia must also continue looking inward. Sabah authorities have conducted hundreds of open-burning prevention patrols, and the latest patrols reportedly found no major fires around several Sabah districts.
The same monitoring showed 182 active hotspots in Kalimantan and 370 in Sumatra, while no hotspots were detected in Sabah.
That matters because Sabahans should not have to bear the consequences of fires we did not start.
And this is ultimately what makes the haze issue more than an environmental problem.
It is a public health issue. A governance issue. An accountability issue.
For Sabahans, especially those living in areas repeatedly affected by haze, it is also a question of whether our concerns receive the same urgency as those elsewhere in Malaysia.

Borneo should not be treated as an afterthought simply because it sits far from the federal administrative centre. The island is shared by countries, states, communities and ecosystems. What happens in Kalimantan can affect Sabah and Sarawak within days. What happens in our forests can affect our neighbours, too.
Borneo does not recognise the borders we drew on a map. Perhaps our policies should stop pretending that it does.
The haze will eventually clear. The skies will become blue again. But if our response remains reactive, we will simply wait for the next dry season, the next fire, and the next unhealthy API reading.
The question is not whether Borneo will face haze again.

It is whether, by then, our governments will finally have the courage to look beyond borders - and hold accountable not only those who light the fires, but those who profit from the land on which they burn.
Because Borneo breathes as one. Our governments, our laws, and our accountability should, too.
Nurul Anna Mausar is a Sabahan law student, youth activist and FMT reader.

Four decades later, in the wake of the 2018 general election, the two parties formalised a renewed alliance, known as Muafakat Nasional which eventually reached an impasse when PAS elected to form Perikatan Nasional alongside Bersatu, a strategic manoeuvre that encountered vehement opposition from Umno.

History has shown that there are no guarantees that an alliance between Umno and PAS would not eventually fall apart.

History has also shown that, although Umno and PAS may draw from the same Malay-Muslim voter base, their relationship has often shifted. They have alternated between working together and confronting each other, depending on changing power dynamics and political survival.
Although “ummah unity” is often invoked to promote political stability, several structural issues could still reignite discord between the two parties.
Demographic and geographic overlap

The two parties have historically engaged in zero-sum competition within the same voter enclaves, specifically rural, Malay-majority constituencies. Consequently, the delineation of parliamentary and state assembly seats regularly precipitates hierarchical friction.
Deadlocks routinely emerge when determining incumbency or candidacy rights in areas designated as "winnable seats", a phenomenon previously observed during initialisation of the MN framework.
Power and leadership hegemony
Establishing the supreme leadership hierarchy, particularly concerning the premiership, remains a highly contentious point of friction.
Should PAS secure a larger parliamentary bloc than Umno, questions over who should lead the alliance could trigger intense internal power struggles and destabilise the partnership.
The trust deficit

Based on past political developments, Umno leaders remain cautious and sceptical of PAS's calls for unity. Sentiments regarding a "breach of trust" are frequently resurrected due to PAS's strategic pivot toward Bersatu within Perikatan Nasional.
This multi-alignment strategy, defined by a propensity to switch partners to secure political survival, directly exacerbates deep-seated institutional mistrust between the two parties.
Ideological divergence
Umno has traditionally leaned toward technocracy, economic development, and state-centric pragmatic policies.
Its political approach is ostensibly secular-nationalist and inclusive, as evidenced by its long-standing history of inter-ethnic cooperation with the MCA and MIC since pre-independence days.

Conversely, PAS prioritises Islamism as its foundational ideology, relying on an electoral doctrine rooted predominantly in a single ethnic demographic. This ideological divergence frequently engenders socio-political polemics during the formulation of public policy.
Strategic dilemma

Umno loyalists and political analysts currently face a strategic dilemma regarding proposed alliances with PAS. Umno's political hegemony since independence has relied substantially on its capacity to capture non-Malay swing votes, particularly in straight-fight scenarios against PAS.
Closer alignment with PAS risks alienating non-Malay voters, a trajectory exemplified by the electoral marginalisation of Gerakan after integrating into PN.

Furthermore, realistic anxieties persist that Umno risks being integrated or subverted by PAS, given that PAS currently commands a superior grassroots machinery and a significantly larger parliamentary presence.

This structural reality threatens to relegate Umno to "junior partner" status, exposing the party to gradual marginalisation compared to the relatively egalitarian power balance they maintained in 2019.
Politics is about pragmatism, meaning no alliance or rivalry lasts forever.
While Umno and PAS possess the capacity to forge new alignments based on the shared imperative of countering a common political enemy, their capacity to sustain such cooperation remains fragile.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

0003a86f9740b0fb: Malaysians recently enjoyed a public holiday on our National Day. Many also enjoyed the week-long school holidays while some got a hattrick of celebrations – an extra day for Selangor residents for the state topping the medals table at the recent Sukma inter-state games.
It’s a pretty good deal for many, including state politicians who got to give out the good news to Selangor’s residents at no cost to themselves because it’s the employers who foot the bill.

As a retiree I didn’t get to enjoy an extra day's holiday nor did I get holiday pay for working on the day. But at least I’m not an employer who has to foot the extra costs or deal with the disruptions caused by it.

Declaring a casual public holiday is a misguided attempt to buy goodwill from the rakyat. Either elections must be around the corner, or it’s become a reflex action for an ad hoc public holiday to be created.

The economy doesn’t benefit from this: costs go up and benefits are reduced to society at large. But you cannot argue about giving workers additional respite from their days at the office or factories. We have laws that require us to observe public holidays, of which we have a lot, scheduled and ad hoc, plus personal paid vacations, with most companies providing more than what is stipulated.

I guess if somebody very important passes away, or we achieve something truly epic – we win the World Cup! – then perhaps a public holiday is deserving. But lets examine the reason public holidays are declared in the first place.

They are meant to allow us to observe such holidays appropriately – perhaps by celebrating, marching in the street, holding celebrations, visiting families and friends or fulfilling cultural or religious obligations.

If you stay at home and don’t celebrate the event, then why are you deserving of a paid day off? I can tell you if Malaysia wins the World Cup I’ll be running myself ragged for perhaps days in an orgy of celebrations, and I certainly would welcome the public holiday.

But I remember a state declared an ad hoc holiday in three consecutive years purely because it made it to the final of the Malaysia Cup football competition. Not won it, just made it to the final, which it managed to lose each time.

I remember the business disruptions, and especially the withering looks from my foreign bosses and colleagues signalling – what kind of rubbish is this? I had no good answer then, and certainly none now either.

Disruptions didn’t just happen to businesses; they happen to normal people too. Most government and business services are closed with hardly any notice. Think about the disruptions to our everyday life in our dealings with the courts or passport offices or many other government as well as commercial services.
Feeling entitled

But the biggest problem is this: the state or national leaders also know we gain nothing from these public holidays. People are not grateful just for an extra day off. They won't work harder when they get back to their workplace, and neither would they change their voting preferences.

We do it because somehow we as the rakyat feel entitled to such perks, and the leaders who declare these holidays feel they are expected to do it, or else they’d be judged negatively if they didn’t oblige with this “generosity”.

Entitlement is becoming a huge problem in Malaysia. We have many things started by the government in good faith, whether affirmative action programmes or economic subsidies for some of the costs of living. Over time, however, these “privileges” have become “rights”, even if none of them have ever been voted in parliament into laws and statues.

When you feel entitled, you feel any questions on your entitlements are wrong or disrespectful or political, or all of them. Logic and justifications go out of the window, and emotions and outrage come into play. This being Malaysia, race and religion often get into the noise and make everything complicated and nasty.

I doubt if the political leaders debate the merits or otherwise on such ad hoc holidays. Most are smart enough to know that the negative impacts outweigh the positive, but somehow feel they’re under pressure to give the rakyat their “entitlement”.

In the end it’s a lose-lose for everybody. Many rakyat get something they haven’t earned, which just motivates them to expect even more unearned goodies. The economic drivers have to absorb the disruptions, and of course pass the negative impacts of higher costs or lower profits back to the population.

We may probably have gone too far down the road for any brave political leaders to say enough with this nonsense. That’s a shame, because we certainly don’t need to add to our growing lists of entitlements. We have more than enough already.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
1eb610b9d5fc900b: Saya amat tertarik dengan kenyataan Hadi dari petikan suatu berita online tentang bagaimana rupanya pemerintahan federal di bawah PAS. Beliau tidak menyebut tentang polisi ekonomi, atau polisi pendidikan, atau polisi sumber manusia, atau polisi alam persekitaran atau polisi mitigasi banjir.

Beliau rumuskan bahawa kepentingan Islam amat perlu dijaga apabila memilih portfolio dan menteri masing-masing supaya orang bukan Islam tak interfere dengan polisi tentang orang Islam.

Yang kedua, kenapa Hadi bangkitkan dua portfolio sahaja sebagai contoh kementerian yang tak perlu ada dasar Islam? Adakah sebab dalam PN ada MIPP dan Gerakan? Maka itu ada seorang menteri India yang bakal menjaga hutan dan seorang menteri Cina yang bakal menjaga jalan raya?

Isu ketiga yang saya nak tanya pula adalah bagaimana Hadi boleh sifatkan yang hutan yang menjadi sebahagian dari alam persekitaran kita sebagai tiada aspek keislamannya? Bukankah dalam al-Quran Allah sentuh banyak tentang sungai, pokok, buah-buahan, bukit bukau untuk menggambarkan nikmatNya kepada manusia dan juga sebagai tanda kebesaran Allah?

Saya selalu bila bersyarah tentang senibina Islam, saya tidak sentuh pasal kubah, gerbang atau menara tetapi saya sering sentuh tentang alam persekitaran ciptaan Tuhan. Maka itu kalau ada arkitek seperti Frank Lloyd Wright yang memang mengagungkan nature, saya kata ini adalah sifat senibina Islam.

Kalau ada Japanese Garden atau Chinese Landscape yang begitu merangsang roh kita melihat dan mengalaminya, saya teringat ayat al-Quran. Bagi saya, National University of Singapore yang saya lawati kelihatan penuh dengan pokok dan kehijauan daun ciptaan Allah dan maka itu saya sifatkan ia adalah lebih Islamic dari kampus UIAM yang kekurangan pokok dan tumbuh-tumbuhan.

Isu keempat adalah menteri di Kementerian Kerja Raya yang boleh dinobatkan orang bukan Islam. Tetapi saya nak tanya Hadi bukankah kementerian itu bertanggungjawab membina sekolah, masjid, bangunan pentadbiran dan banyak lagi. Tidakkah bangunan-bangunan ini dihuni dan diguna oleh orang Islam juga secara majoritinya? Kalau begitu bagaimana dikatakan tiada langsung dasar Islam padanya?

Isu kelima adalah kementerian mana lagi yang ‘tak ada kena mengena dengan dasar Islam’? Terdapat 28 kementerian masa kini. Saya nak juga tahu kementerian mana lagi yang Hadi maksudkan untuk meletakkan orang bukan Islam? Sefaham saya kesemua kementerian memang ada dasar yang boleh dibuat berkait dengan orang Islam.

Semasa saya belajar tentang Islamic Reform, Islam itu Syumul dan bermaksud menyeluruh dan merangkumi semua. What happened to that concept? Adakah dua kementerian yang disebut Hadi itu saja yang akan diberikan kepada menteri bukan Islam?

Saya hendak tahu kementerian-kementerian mana lagi yang boleh dipimpin oleh non-Muslim dalam PN. Jawatan untuk presiden MIPP dan Gerakan nampak gayanya dah ada. Tahniah mereka berdua. Jawatan nak bagi MCA dan MIC bila bergabung dengan BN, nak letak kat mana?

Isu keenam adalah tentang style kepimpinan. Hadi berkata bahawa sebagai pemimpin individu itulah bertanggungjawab untuk membuat polisi. Saya rasa Hadi mungkin confuse kepimpinan professional dan kepimpinan kelas agama atau madrasah

Kepimpinan agama mungkin mengambil corak authoritarian atau konsep Tok Guru di mana individu itu berkuasa penuh dan orang lain tak boleh soal. Pengurusan professional mengambil pendekatan mendengar penasihat-penasihat dan juga pandangan-pandangan dalam mesyuarat sebelum mengambil keputusan untuk bertindak by consensus, by majority atau Chairman boleh mengambil keputusan unilateral atau ‘ikut cakap aku’.

Kalau menggunakan pendekatan pengurusan professional maka sesiapa pun boleh menjadi menteri, tidak perlu dari satu agama atau kaum. Kecualilah kementerian wanita dan keluarga, sebab ada perkataan wanita, maka kena lah bersifat gender centric.
Akhir sekali saya nak berpesan kepada Umno sebelum dia sign marriage contract. Adakah Umno benar-benar nak menikah dengan PAS untuk duduk serumah dalam kerajaan federal?

Kita dah nampak PAS punya cara mengurus negara dari kenyataan Hadi. Adakah Umno pun agak mengikut rentak beliau dalam mengisi individu dan portfolio kementerian nanti? Zahid dulu saya ingat dia seorang guru di Yayasan Anda. Bolehkah guru counter arahan ayahanda Tok Guru agama?
Bagi kita rakyat Malaysia, kena bersedialah untuk mempunyai kerajaan ala-madrasah untuk kita maju ke depan atau ke belakang.

5122b4c7a7f37db0: In the last five years, six youth-led, anti-establishment uprisings have fundamentally reshaped South Asia’s political landscape.

The movements had much in common: they all reflected young people’s aspirations, digital savvy, economic frustrations, and disillusionment with governing elites. But the political systems in which they unfolded process grievances in vastly different ways, leading to sharply divergent outcomes.

The story begins in Myanmar, where the military’s February 2021 overthrow of a democratically elected government triggered popular protests. Unconstrained by concerns about democratic legitimacy, the new regime launched a violent crackdown.

With the peaceful restoration of democracy off the table, a generation of young people had little choice but to form civilian defense forces alongside armed ethnically based organisations. The result was a grinding civil war.

Sri Lanka’s March 2022 Aragalaya movement arose from economic collapse. Dry fuel pumps, prolonged power cuts, and sovereign insolvency destroyed the legitimacy of the Rajapaksa dynasty, which had ruled for the better part of two decades. Protests roiled the island, with demonstrators eventually occupying the presidential palace.

Yet, unlike Myanmar, Sri Lanka did not face surging violence, let alone a prolonged armed conflict. Instead, president Gotabaya Rajapaksa submitted to popular pressure and resigned within the constitutional framework.

In Pakistan, riots erupted in May 2023, following the arrest of former prime minister Imran Khan. This was a case of a populist movement mobilising behind a charismatic leader to challenge the military’s dominance—and it was met with a troop deployment, an internet shutdown, and the dismantling of the opposition’s formal party structures. The “hybrid” regime was preserved, at the cost of persistent political alienation.
Bangladesh’s July 2024 uprising demonstrated how a narrow policy dispute—in this case, student opposition to a skewed quota system for civil-service jobs—can turn into a revolution.
As protests against prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s autocratic regime escalated, Hasina deployed troops to enforce a curfew—with an order to shoot violators on sight.
When the military ultimately refused, Hasina’s hold on power collapsed. She fled the country, opening the way for an interim government to take over.

In Nepal, the September 2025 protests targeted not a single leader, but an oligarchic political class, which had been playing a decade-long game of prime ministerial “musical chairs” while most Nepali youths struggled with soaring unemployment and a lack of opportunity.
For a frustrated Gen Z, a government ban on major social-media platforms was the last straw: using VPNs and alternative apps, Nepal’s youth organised a massive protest.

The authorities attempted to crush it by force, but the protesters fought back, driving the elites out without destroying the parliamentary framework. Nepalis went on to elect a 35-year-old prime minister.
Finally, this summer, India experienced widespread student-led protests, sparked by leaks of university entrance examinations and fuelled by growing anxiety over jobless growth.

Far from threatening the constitutional order, however, the movement confirmed that order’s resilience, as the government offered critical concessions, accepting the education minister’s resignation and proposing administrative and policy reforms with a view towards redirecting protest energy back through established democratic channels.

These six cases show that hyper-connectivity and economic and political alienation are a potent combination. The first fully digitally native generation, Gen Z uses platforms like TikTok, WhatsApp, and Discord to bypass entrenched party structures and orchestrate mass mobilisations.
But that is not all that stands out about Gen Z’s protest style. Unlike their predecessors, today’s protesters are motivated by a sense that they have nothing to lose.

It is not hard to see why: with their economic prospects drastically diminished, despite high educational attainment, what today’s young people see are not flawed institutions in need of reform, but a predatory system robbing them of a viable future.

This imbues their protests with a visceral, existential urgency and makes them resistant to state co-optation. Unimpressed by incremental concessions, they are willing to confront institutional repression head-on.

For all they have in common, these six cases also underscore the difference institutional structures make. In closed regimes that treat power as non-negotiable, such as Myanmar and Pakistan, popular discontent inevitably results in political fragmentation or chronic instability.

In rigid civilian autocracies like Hasina’s Bangladesh, protest is either repressed or revolutionary: the system is unmovable until a single crack—such as the military refusing an order—brings down the whole edifice.
Conversely, systems that allow for political transitions or administrative conciliation can survive generational shocks.

Sri Lanka achieved a peaceful electoral realignment, and Nepal engineered a political reset, which created space for “outsider” political forces. India, for its part, showed how a robust multiparty democracy accommodates discontent before it metastasizes into systemic crisis.

These episodes hold several important lessons. For starters, celebrating aggregate macroeconomic growth but ignoring youth unemployment and systemic corruption is a recipe for instability. Younger generations view economic opportunity as inseparable from political accountability—and they will, sooner or later, demand both.

Moreover, military-dominated governance is poorly suited for this era of hyper-connectivity. While crackdowns and coercion can suppress dissent temporarily, they destroy state legitimacy over time. Relying on them risks prolonged civil disorder.

Finally, dismantling systemic corruption is only the first step. Durable institutions, with democratic pressure valves and credible mechanisms for addressing young people’s aspirations, are also essential.
That is why India’s recent uprising reaffirmed its democracy, while Nepal and Sri Lanka, as well as Bangladesh, have faced considerable post-uprising instability.

The Arab Spring revolutions a decade and a half ago ultimately ended in military counter-revolution, autocratic revival, or institutional paralysis, owing to absent or fragile democratic legacies and ideological hijacking. But many South Asian societies possess deep parliamentary traditions, vibrant civil societies, and functional constitutional mechanisms.

If South Asian countries can harness young people’s activist energy to deliver effective, responsive governance and job-creating reforms, they will put themselves on a path towards a brighter, more resilient, and more prosperous future. And they will become a model for how the Global South can align demographic weight with democratic accountability.

Shashi Tharoor, a former UN under-secretary-general and former Indian minister of state for external affairs and minister of state for human resource development, is a fourth-term elected member of Parliament for the opposition Indian National Congress.

bfdce3ac86d9c7bc: Kehebatan Tun M dalam politik memang tidak ada siapa yang boleh tandingi. Sama ada beliau berkuasa atau tidak, gelagat dan kata dua beliau akan sering menjadi buah mulut rakyat sekalian. Itu hebatnya Mahathir.

Beliau tidak perlu guna ayat al-Quran langsung dan tidak perlu ceramah berjela-jela dalam Facebook, cuma datang, duduk atas kerusi roda dan senyum sambil melambai. Itu pun sudah cukup untuk memulakan ribut taufan bersama halilintar.

Kenapa Tun M tak dijemput secara rasmi, 'sound' beberapa influencer yang becok berceloteh. Inikan suatu ketidakadilan kepada seorang tokoh negara? Sebenarnya saya pun agak setuju dengan teguran ini tetapi ada lima perkara yang perlu kita semua renungi dahulu.

Perkara pertama adalah apa yang disebut oleh Rafizi dalam podcastnya bila ditanya tentang isu ini. Saya berterima kasih dengan Rafizi yang memberi maklumat yang kita semua pun tak tahu. Kata Rafizi, Tun M sendiri yang mengubah protokol menjemput bekas perdana menteri untuk majlis penting seperti merdeka pada 2018.

Rafizi memberi alasan takkanlah Tun M nak duduk sebelah seorang penjenayah dan seteru beliau. Tetapi ada influencer yang tegur, Najib belum penjenayah lagi sebab baru buka kes. So, what’s the problem? Yang penting, seperti biasa, Tun memang bijak baling batu dan sembunyi tangan sambil senyum dan melambai.

Perkara kedua, kalaulah kita ada protokol untuk menjemput bekas perdana menteri atau kita ikut adab Melayu lah untuk jemput orang besar-besar, I must assume yang protokol tu dibuat dengan anggapan bahawa bekas perdana menteri tidak lagi berpolitik.

Dalam kes Tun M, beliau masih giat berpolitik dan rasanya sanggup memegang tampuk kerajaan sebagai PM untuk kali ketiga! Jadi, kalau begini rupanya, patutkah PM sedia ada menjemput seterunya dalam politik ke pentas Merdeka?

Perkara ketiga pula adalah Tun M telah membuat naratif bahawa Melayu akan hilang kuasa kalau tidak duduk di bawah satu payung besar. Sudah tentulah, payung tu dia yang punya. Jadi kalau semua Melayu duduk di situ kita boleh teka tiga kali siapa akan jadi PM.

Namun demikian, apa yang saya gusarkan adalah dengan membina naratif ini maka ia membuat suatu permusuhan dengan rakyat lain bukan Melayu termasuk Bumiputra semua. Patutkah seorang bekas PM yang menerajui negara dua kali dan masih membina naratif permusuhan antara Melayu dan bukan Melayu dijemput ke pentas duduk bersama parti PH yang tidak pernah menggunakan ras atau isu perkauman?
Saya pun tidak tergamak untuk duduk sebelah orang sebegini, tidak kisah lah dia PM berapa kali pun. Orang yang membuat kita bermusuh-musuh, bagi saya batang tubuh itu lah musuh terbesar negara kita.

Nasib baik Tun M tidak jadi seperti seorang guru agama yang nak buat kita bermusuh antara orang Islam dan bukan Islam, yang itu lagi ‘haru’ kata orang utara. Saya rasa Tun M baik sikit daripada tok guru agama yang pandai tafsir Quran ikut suka dia.

Perkara keempat adalah Tun M telah pernah membuat naratif Malaysia ini bukan negara multicultural sebab tidak ada disebutkan dalam konsep Malaysia secara undang-undang. Sekali lagi beliau memainkan isu ‘pendatang’ dan memainkan lagu lama bahawa pendatang akan take over everything kalau Melayu tak sedar dan tak bersatu. Same old song but very efective still.

Maklumlah orang Melayu ramai tidak belajar falsafah dan sejarah peradaban dunia. Kebanyakan Melayu belajar kejuruteraan, seni bina, perubatan, undang-undang dan bila pencen baru mengadap kuliah agama.

Mahathir adalah seorang pembaca tegar dan dia faham selok belok sejarah Malaysia dan dunia. Sejarah subjek kegemarannya, saya baca dalam buku beliau A Doctor in the House. Saya memang baca banyak buku Tun M, saya rasa empat buah kesemuanya. Jadi, kita kena tanya diri kita sebagai rakyat, do we want someone yang tidak admit kita negara multicultural?

Perkara kelima, memanglah dari satu sudut, kita patut jemput orang tua itu. Memang kita patut honor seorang pemimpin seperti Tun M. Tetapi jika batang tubuh itu sendiri bergerak untuk mengkucar-kacirkan kita semua, what should we do?

Pada 2016, Tun M berkempen untuk menyelamatkan Malaysia daripada perompak 1MDB. Beliau ke hulu dan ke hilir menjaja Malaysia bakal bankrap dengan si perompak ini. Bagi saya, we owe Tun M a debt of gratitude sebab dengan kempen itu kita rakyat dapat menumbangkan Umno sebagai gergasi berkuasa.

Dalam bab itu, Tun M memainkan peranan kita sebagai a united rakyat to save our country. Tetapi apabila beliau memainkan sentimen perkauman untuk menjatuhkan kerajaan perpaduan, that is an entirely different matter.

Maka itu, kita kena renung sendiri sama ada kita nak bagi hormat atau tidak kepada orang seperti Tun M. Saya sendiri amat menghormati beliau dalam banyak perkara seperti ketegasan beliau tentang ekstremis agama, tentang menimba ilmu dan memahirkan diri dalam sains, teknologi dan Bahasa Inggeris.

Tetapi saya tidak akan berkompromi kepada sesiapa pun yang cuba menjurangkan hubungan baik kita sebagai rakyat Malaysia dengan meniup bahang kaum, agama atau sejarah.That is the line I will not allow anyone to cross.
Itu jalur pemisah antara Merdeka sebagai rakyat dengan mereka yang nak menjatuhkan idea negara-bangsa kita.

a4b3f6287a5a5dbc: Saya mengikuti muktamar PAS yang sedang berlangsung di Pengkalan Chepa, Kelantan dari jauh. Ramai yang hadir dan ramai juga wakil yang berpidato dan dari situ, banyak persoalan yang timbul di benak saya.
Saya tidak banyak mendengar ucapan khusus tentang masalah negeri atau negara, apalagi tentang hal-hal yang berkait dengan ekonomi rakyat atau ekonomi negara.

Ataupun tentang hutang negara yang begitu tinggi, masalah kewangan defisit, perbelanjaan kerajaan berlebihan, Belanjawan 2027, pembahagian hasil dan pendapatan, serta bagaimana semua ini akan diuruskan sekiranya PAS mengambil alih tampuk pemerintahan negara.

Persoalan saya di sini, bukan sekadar sama ada PAS mampu memenangi pilihan raya akan datang dan membentuk kerajaan. Mereka yang hadir nampaknya percaya dan agak yakin. Sebagai contoh, 'Time for PAS to lead with its own PM candidate, says youth leader', satu impian besar yang perlu sedikit kajian dan penjelasan.
Persoalan yang lebih besar ialah: adakah PAS benar-benar mempunyai keupayaan, kepakaran dan kerangka dasar yang jelas untuk mentadbir sebuah negara majmuk?

Berapa ramai pakar ekonomi, tokoh fiskal atau kewangan, perdagangan, pendidikan, industri, pengangkutan dan pembangunan dalam PAS? Apakah mereka sekadar bergantung harap kepada rakan politiknya semata-mata?

Siapa dalam kalangan mereka yang berkaliber untuk membentuk dasar baharu? Siapakah antara yang hadir, mampu melakukan perubahan pengurusan negara supaya Malaysia bukan sekadar ditadbir, tetapi benar-benar dimajukan ke tahap yang lebih baik dan lebih tinggi?
Memerintah Malaysia bukan hanya sekadar menjadi perdana menteri, menteri atau timbalan menteri.

Ia memerlukan satu pasukan yang mempunyai kepakaran, pengalaman dan keberanian untuk membuat keputusan yang sukar, khususnya apabila berhadapan dengan masalah fiskal, hutang negara, subsidi, pelaburan, perdagangan, pendidikan, hubungan antarabangsa dan hubungan antara kerajaan persekutuan dengan Sabah dan Sarawak.
Rakyat perlu tahu apakah sebenarnya visi dan misi PAS untuk Malaysia.
Dasar fiskal
Pada pandangan saya, antara perkara paling penting yang akan menentukan kejayaan atau kegagalan mana-mana kerajaan baharu ialah dasar fiskal mereka.

Dasar fiskal ini menentukan bagaimana kerajaan memperolehi hasil, siapa yang membayar cukai, bagaimana wang dibelanjakan, siapa yang menerima bantuan dan bagaimana defisit serta hutang negara dikawal, menjadi seimbang atau ada lebihan (surplus). Di sinilah PAS perlu memberikan perhatian utama dengan pandangan yang pandai, padat dan serius.

Cadangan “Please change the movie on tax” oleh Geoffrey Williams, misalnya, merupakan satu cadangan dasar fiskal yang menarik dan wajar diberi perhatian. Tiada seorang pun yang hadir di muktamar PAS menyentuh tentang hal yang penting seperti ini.
Cadangan menggunakan electronic payment tax (EPT) sebagai mekanisme percukaian baharu, jika dilaksanakan dengan reka bentuk yang betul, berpotensi mengubah cara kerajaan mengutip hasil.

Sekiranya PAS benar-benar mahu memimpin Putrajaya, saya berpendapat mereka perlu mendengar pandangan pakar seperti beliau dan pakar-pakar dari kaum lain yang mempunyai kepakaran dalam percukaian dan kewangan awam. Persoalannya ialah: apakah model percukaian alternatif yang PAS mahu dan akan diperkenalkan?

Adakah PAS akan terus bergantung kepada sistem cukai sedia ada (SST dan GST) atau mempunyai keberanian untuk memperkenalkan pendekatan baharu yang lebih luas asasnya, lebih cekap kutipannya dan lebih adil kepada rakyat?

Jika EPT mampu direka dengan baik sehingga kutipan hasil kerajaan menjadi lebih cekap tanpa terlalu membebankan golongan berpendapatan rendah, ia boleh menjadi sebahagian daripada reset fiskal negara. Tetapi ini memerlukan kajian, kepakaran dan perancangan yang sangat teliti.

Kerajaan tetap memerlukan hasil yang mencukupi untuk membiayai kos pengurusan, belanjawan untuk pendidikan, kesihatan, keselamatan, pengangkutan awam, infrastruktur dan pembangunan negara. Justeru, PAS perlu menjelaskan bukan sahaja berapa banyak cukai yang mahu dikutip, tetapi daripada siapa, dengan cara bagaimana dan untuk membiayai apa.
Defisit, hutang dan ketirisan

Terkait dengan dasar fiskal ialah belanjawan defisit Malaysia setiap tahun yang telah melangkau lebih dua puluh lapan tahun, sejak 1998. Belanjawan defisit ini membuatkan hutang kerajaan terus meningkat, yang kini sudah melebihi RM1.38 trilion atau sejumlah 64% daripada kadar Keluaran Dalam Negara Kasar. Dalam keadaan sebegini, setiap ringgit wang negara dan wang rakyat sepatutnya diurus dengan penuh amanah, telus dan berdisiplin. Ini yang harus disahut oleh PAS.

Masalahnya bukan sekadar kerajaan berbelanja terlalu banyak. Persoalan yang lebih besar ialah ke mana wang itu dibelanjakan, berapa banyak yang benar-benar sampai kepada rakyat dan berapa banyak yang hilang akibat ketirisan, pembaziran, penyelewengan, rasuah dan salah guna kuasa.

Sebab itu, jika PAS benar-benar serius untuk mengambil alih Putrajaya, rakyat berhak menuntut satu kenyataan dan pendirian yang jelas, tegas dan tidak berkompromi mengenai rasuah dan salah guna kuasa, khususnya apabila ia melibatkan wang negara dan wang simpanan rakyat.

Tanpa kenyataan yang kukuh dan meyakinkan mengenai perkara ini, pendirian PAS boleh ditafsirkan sebagai tidak serius, lemah dan akhirnya memudaratkan negara. Apalagi di muktamar kali ini, PAS mengundang parti-parti politik yang terjebak dengan gejala rasuah dan salahguna kuasa tersebut.
Ini bukan lagi soal politik kepartian atau rakan kongsi politik. Ini soal wang negara dan wang rakyat, yang memerlukan kerangka polisi yang wajar dan kuat.

Apabila negara mempunyai hutang yang begitu besar dan terus berbelanja dalam keadaan belanjawan defisit, kerajaan tidak boleh pada masa yang sama membiarkan ruang untuk ketirisan, pembaziran dan penyelewengan terus terbuka dan berlaku.

Setiap ketirisan akhirnya perlu dibayar oleh rakyat -- sama ada melalui cukai yang lebih tinggi, pengurangan subsidi, pengurangan perkhidmatan awam, pinjaman baharu atau hutang yang akan ditanggung oleh generasi akan datang.
Oleh itu, PAS perlu menjelaskan dengan terang empat tunggak utama:

• Apakah langkah konkrit yang akan diambil untuk membanteras rasuah? • Apakah mekanisme yang akan digunapakai untuk menutup ruang ketirisan? • Apakah dasar baru yang akan diperkenalkan terhadap sistem perolehan kerajaan? • Apakah tindakan yang akan diambil terhadap mereka yang menyalahgunakan kuasa, termasuk jika mereka datang daripada parti atau gabungan politik sendiri?

Empat persoalan dan jawapan dari pihak PAS ini sangat penting. Rakyat tidak mahu mendengar janji membanteras rasuah hanya ketika PAS menjadi pembangkang. Rakyat mahu melihat apakah prinsip yang sama akan digunakan apabila PAS menjadi kerajaan dan berhadapan dengan pesalah dari orang dalam kalangan mereka sendiri atau rakan politik mereka. Yang salah, tetap salah, sama ada kawan atau lawan.

Berhubung gejala rasuah, kenyataan presiden PAS dimuktamar semalam tidak memberansangkan. Sila lihat 'Corruption in Malaysia weaponised to discredit rivals, claims Hadi'. Apakah kerajaan PAS kelak tidak akan menutup segala kebocoran dan ketirisan dalam sistem kewangan negara?
Jika kebocoran tidak ditutup, berapa banyak pun hasil yang dikutip, negara akan terus menghadapi masalah yang sama, tidak kira pesalahnya menganut agama apa sekalipun.

Ia bukan lagi isu moral semata-mata. Ia adalah isu ekonomi, isu kekuatan kewangan negara dan ianya juga, adalah isu masa depan generasi muda Malaysia. Sebab itu, isu gejala rasuah, ketirisan dan salah guna kuasa amat penting untuk dijadikan landasan sebenar polisi parti dan ia merangkumi sebahagian daripada dasar fiskal dan kewangan negara.
Jadi sebelum PAS meminta rakyat memberikan mandat untuk memimpin Putrajaya, mereka perlu terlebih dahulu menjawab satu soalan yang mudah tetapi sangat besar maknanya:
Apakah sebenarnya rancangan fiskal PAS untuk Malaysia?
